Existence Of Circumcenter

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move a triangle's corners and watch the lines through the small dots meet at one place.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Slide the three dots onto the middles of their sides to draw the circle; the buttons reset the picture and hide the names.
Look for the math

Mark the middles of two sides of a triangle and draw a line straight out from each. The two lines always cross, and the crossing point is the centre of a circle through all three corners. This is Euclid IV.5, and there is no winning or losing here — just a picture you can test.

A line of equal distances

The perpendicular bisector of a segment is the place of points equally far from its two ends. In the picture, N sits on AB and M on AC. When a dot reaches its side's midpoint, its line is that bisector, so any point O on it has AO = BO and AO = CO. The page names M and N in the opposite order from the segments it bisects; the equality is the same either way.

One point, three equal distances

The two bisectors have one meeting point O. From the first line AO = BO; from the second AO = CO. By transitivity, BO = CO too. So all three distances are equal, and a circle centred at O with that radius goes through A, B and C. That circle is the circumcircle and O is the circumcenter. The logic test checks these equalities, and that the circle passes through all three vertices, on more than eighteen thousand triangles.

Inside, on a side, or outside

The page says the two lines may meet inside the triangle, on the side BC, or outside BC. All three really happen: a triangle with a sharp angle at A keeps O inside; a right angle at A puts O at the midpoint of BC; an obtuse angle at A sends O outside. The logic test checks that the place of O follows the size of angle A over the whole grid of triangles and hundreds of random ones.

What the dots are doing

The applet lets you slide L, M and N along their sides and only draws the circle once all three are within 2 pixels of the true midpoints. It also draws the third bisector, through L, although the page only needs two. We keep that behaviour and add a button that places all three dots exactly, so the circle can be seen without a steady hand. A triangle whose three corners lie on one straight line has no circle: the applet stops drawing there.

Try a triangle with a right angle at A, then pull A past a right angle and watch O cross the side BC and move away outside.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
